pharm: Long-acting recombinant human insulin analog that forms soluble multihexamers after subcutaneous injection, providing a flat, ultra-long glucose-lowering effect lasting beyond 42 hours.
quick: Insulin-naive type 2: 10 units once daily; type 1: as part of total daily insulin (basal ~one-third to one-half of 0.2-0.4 units/kg)
Subcutaneous injection any time of day; not tied to meals
Clinical data show no clear maternal/fetal risk; manage to maintain tight glycemic control
Endogenous-like insulin; considered compatible with breastfeeding
No specific dose adjustment, but monitor closely - hypoglycemia risk increases
No specific dose adjustment, but monitor closely - hypoglycemia risk increases
Increases hypoglycemia risk and may mask warning signs - use cautiously
Blood glucose, HbA1c, hypoglycemia signs, potassium during dose changes
summary: Insulin degludec is an ultra-long-acting basal insulin analog used to improve glycemic control in patients 1 year of age and older with type 1 or type 2 diabetes mellitus. After subcutaneous injection it forms soluble multihexamers that slowly dissociate, giving a flat, peakless profile with a half-life of about 25 hours and glucose-lowering action lasting beyond 42 hours, allowing once-daily dosing with flexible timing. The recommended starting dose in insulin-naive type 2 diabetes is 10 units once daily; in type 1 diabetes it provides the basal component (about one-third to one-half) of a total daily dose of roughly 0.2-0.4 units/kg. It is not for treating diabetic ketoacidosis. Hypoglycemia is the most common and potentially serious adverse effect.
indications: To improve glycemic control in patients 1 year of age and older with type 1 diabetes mellitus
To improve glycemic control in patients 1 year of age and older with type 2 diabetes mellitus

dosage.d: Starting dose 10 units once daily; titrate based on glucose targets
Total daily insulin ~0.2-0.4 units/kg; give about one-third to one-half as basal degludec, remainder as mealtime insulin
Start at the same unit dose as the total daily long/intermediate-acting insulin previously used
When transitioning, reduce total daily insulin to decrease hypoglycemia risk; individualize

admin: Inject subcutaneously into the thigh, upper arm, or abdomen; rotate injection sites within a region
May be given at any time of day, but maintain at least 8 hours between doses; flexible timing is allowed
Do NOT administer intravenously, intramuscularly, or in an insulin pump
Do not mix or dilute with any other insulin or solution
Inspect that the solution is clear and colorless before use; never share pens between patients
moa: Insulin degludec is a long-acting basal human insulin analog that, like endogenous insulin, lowers blood glucose by binding insulin receptors on muscle and fat to stimulate peripheral glucose uptake and by inhibiting hepatic glucose production. Its prolonged action results from the formation of soluble multihexamers at the subcutaneous injection site that slowly and continuously release insulin degludec monomers into the circulation, where they also reversibly bind albumin - producing a flat, ultra-long, peakless pharmacodynamic profile with low day-to-day variability.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to insulin degludec or any of its excipients
relative: Renal or hepatic impairment (increased hypoglycemia risk - monitor and titrate carefully)
Conditions causing hypokalemia or concomitant potassium-lowering drugs
Acute illness, stress, or changes in physical activity/diet (alter insulin requirements)
monitor: Blood glucose, especially during dose titration and intercurrent illness

preg: Clinical trial data in pregnant women with type 1 diabetes showed no clear evidence of maternal or fetal risk associated with insulin degludec. Poorly controlled diabetes in pregnancy poses risks to mother and fetus; maintain good glycemic control. Insulin requirements typically change across trimesters and require dose adjustment.
lact: Insulin degludec, like endogenous insulin, is presumed compatible with breastfeeding; any insulin in milk is digested and not systemically absorbed by the infant. Breastfeeding may alter maternal insulin requirements.
renal: No specific dosage adjustment is required for renal impairment, but the risk of hypoglycemia is increased; intensify glucose monitoring and titrate the dose carefully.
hepatic: No specific dosage adjustment is required for hepatic impairment, but the risk of hypoglycemia is increased; intensify glucose monitoring and titrate the dose carefully.

major: Other glucose-lowering agents (sulfonylureas, other insulins, GLP-1 agonists) - additive hypoglycemia risk
Thiazolidinediones - increased risk of fluid retention and heart failure when combined with insulin
moderate: Beta-blockers, clonidine, guanethidine, reserpine - may mask signs of hypoglycemia
Corticosteroids, thiazides, atypical antipsychotics, sympathomimetics, thyroid hormone - may reduce glucose-lowering effect
ACE inhibitors, fibrates, fluoxetine, MAO inhibitors, salicylates, sulfonamide antibiotics - may enhance glucose-lowering effect
minor: Pentamidine - may cause hypoglycemia followed by hyperglycemia
interactions.food: Take any time of day independent of meals; maintain consistent carbohydrate intake to support stable glucose control.
interactions.alcohol: Alcohol can increase or prolong the glucose-lowering effect and may blunt hypoglycemia warning signs; use cautiously and with food.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause hypokalemia; relevant for potassium monitoring and ECG interpretation in at-risk patients.

serious: Severe hypoglycemia (may cause seizures, loss of consciousness, death)
Fluid retention and heart failure when used with thiazolidinediones
rare: Lipoatrophy or lipohypertrophy at injection sites
emergency: Severe hypoglycemia with confusion, seizure, or coma

monitoring: Self-monitored blood glucose and HbA1c to guide titration
Serum potassium in patients at risk for hypokalemia
Signs and symptoms of hypoglycemia, especially during dose changes, illness, or activity changes
Injection sites for lipodystrophy; rotate sites
Renal and hepatic function, which influence insulin requirements
counsel: Inject once a day at a time you can keep consistent; you may vary the time but keep at least 8 hours between doses
Never inject this insulin into a vein or muscle, do not use it in a pump, and do not mix it with other insulins
Know the signs of low blood sugar (shakiness, sweating, confusion) and always carry a fast-acting sugar source
Rotate injection sites to avoid lumps or pitting in the skin; never share your pen with anyone
Tell your doctor about illness, changes in diet/exercise, or other diabetes medicines, as your dose may need adjusting
pk: Gradual; steady-state plasma concentrations reached after 2-3 days of once-daily dosing
Essentially peakless (flat profile); maximum glucose-lowering effect at a median of ~12 hours
Unopened: refrigerate 2-8 C (36-46 F), do not freeze. In-use pen/vial: room temperature up to 30 C (86 F) for up to 8 weeks; protect from light/heat
pearls: Ultra-long, flat, peakless basal insulin (half-life ~25 hours, duration >42 hours) allows flexible once-daily timing - convenient when dose times vary
Hypoglycemia is the most common and most serious adverse effect; risk rises with renal/hepatic impairment, alcohol, and other glucose-lowering drugs
Available in U100 and U200 concentrations - the pen delivers the correct dose; no unit conversion is needed, but verify concentration to avoid errors
Not for diabetic ketoacidosis or hyperglycemic emergencies (use rapid-acting IV insulin instead)
Insulin can shift potassium intracellularly - watch for hypokalemia, especially with concomitant potassium-lowering drugs
missed: If a dose is missed, inject it as soon as remembered as long as at least 8 hours can elapse before the next scheduled dose, then resume the regular once-daily schedule. Never inject two doses within 8 hours or double a dose to make up for a missed one. Monitor blood glucose more closely after a missed or delayed dose.
overdose: Insulin overdose causes hypoglycemia, which may be severe and life-threatening (seizures, coma) and hypokalemia. Treat mild hypoglycemia with oral glucose/carbohydrate; treat severe episodes with intravenous glucose and/or glucagon, and correct potassium. Because of the ultra-long duration of action, prolonged monitoring and repeated glucose administration may be required.
